questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is 'The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.' Who said it, and in which work?

options.text: Edgar Codd, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970)
Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1922)
Alan Kay, The Early History of Smalltalk (1993)
Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming (1968)

questions.explanation: It sets up the chapter's first-paragraph claim: data models affect not just how the software is written but how we think about the problem we are solving.

questions.question: The chapter names two distinct effects a data model has. Which two? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: How the software is written
How we think about the problem we are solving
How fast the hardware executes queries
How much disk the data consumes

questions.explanation: Most readers remember only the first. The second is the epigraph's point and the reason the chapter exists.

questions.question: Most applications are built by layering one data model on another. What is the single key question the chapter says you ask at each layer?

options.text: How fast is it?
How is it represented in terms of the next-lower layer?
Who owns this layer?
Can it be replaced?

questions.explanation: Each layer hides the complexity of the layers below it by providing a clean data model.

questions.question: Order the chapter's four layers from highest to lowest.

options.text: Application objects and data structures; a general-purpose data model (JSON, tables, graph); bytes in memory, on disk, or on a network; electrical currents, pulses of light, magnetic fields
A general-purpose data model; application objects; bytes; electrical currents
Bytes; application objects; a general-purpose data model; electrical currents
Electrical currents; bytes; a general-purpose data model; application objects

questions.explanation: The application layer is often specific to your application; the general-purpose data model may allow the data to be queried, searched, manipulated, and processed.

questions.question: What organizational benefit does the chapter claim from layering?

options.text: It reduces the number of engineers needed
It allows different groups of people — for example, the engineers at the database vendor and the application developers using their database — to work together effectively
It makes systems faster
It eliminates the need for documentation

questions.explanation: The clean data model between layers is what makes the division of labour possible.

questions.question: 'Every data model embodies assumptions about how it is going to be used.' Which pairs of consequences does the chapter spell out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some kinds of usage are easy, others are not supported
Some operations are fast, others perform badly
Some data transformations feel natural, others are awkward
Some models are cheap, others require licensing

questions.explanation: Which is why there are many different kinds of data models, and why choosing the right one matters.

questions.question: Which layer does Chapter 2 cover, and which does Chapter 3 cover?

options.text: Chapter 2 covers the application object layer; Chapter 3 covers the general-purpose data model
Chapter 2 covers the general-purpose data model (point 2); Chapter 3 covers how it is represented in bytes (point 3)
Chapter 2 covers bytes; Chapter 3 covers hardware
Both cover the same layer at different depths

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 is the data model; Chapter 3 is storage and retrieval — how the model is represented at the next layer down.

questions.question: Give the relational model's own terms, their SQL equivalents, and the property the chapter is careful to mention.

options.text: Relations become tables and tuples become rows; a relation is an unordered collection of tuples. Codd proposed the model in 1970
Relations become rows and tuples become tables; a relation is an ordered collection. Codd proposed it in 1980
Relations become schemas and tuples become columns; ordering is significant
Relations become indexes and tuples become keys; the collection is sorted by key

questions.explanation: Unorderedness is load-bearing: it is exactly what lets the query optimizer reorder work, as the declarative-query section later argues.

questions.question: What were relational databases originally used for, and why does the chapter call those uses 'mundane from today's perspective'?

options.text: Scientific computing on supercomputers
Business data processing on mainframes in the 1960s and '70s — transaction processing and batch processing — yet the model turned out to generalize very well, beyond its original scope
Military logistics, which required unusual reliability
Early web applications

questions.explanation: The point is the generalization: the workloads were unglamorous but the abstraction outlived them.

questions.question: What did other databases of the relational era force developers to do, and how does that frame the relational model's goal?

options.text: They forced developers to think about the internal representation of the data in the database — so the relational model's goal was to hide that implementation detail behind a cleaner interface
They forced developers to write SQL by hand
They forced developers to manage transactions manually
They forced developers to shard data across machines

questions.explanation: The relational model was an abstraction play from the start.

questions.question: Match each challenger to its era: the network and hierarchical models, object databases, XML databases.

options.text: Network/hierarchical in the 1970s and early 1980s; object databases in the late 1980s and early 1990s; XML databases in the early 2000s
Object databases in the 1970s; network/hierarchical in the 1990s; XML in 2010s
XML in the 1980s; object databases in the 1990s; network/hierarchical in the 2000s
All three emerged simultaneously in the 1990s

questions.explanation: Object databases came and went again; XML databases have only seen niche adoption. Each competitor generated a lot of hype in its time, but it never lasted.

questions.question: What happened to computing that could have killed relational databases, and what happened instead?

options.text: As computers became vastly more powerful and networked, they started being used for increasingly diverse purposes — and relational databases turned out to generalize very well beyond business data processing
Disks became cheap, so normalization stopped mattering
SQL was standardized, locking in the incumbent
Mainframes were replaced by minicomputers, which only ran relational software

questions.explanation: Generalization, not lock-in, is the chapter's explanation for the relational model's survival.

questions.question: Where did the name 'NoSQL' actually come from?

options.text: A 1998 research paper on non-relational storage
A Twitter hashtag for a meetup on open source, distributed, nonrelational databases in 2009 — later retroactively reinterpreted as 'Not Only SQL'
A marketing campaign by MongoDB
An internal Google codename

questions.explanation: The chapter calls the name unfortunate, since it describes what the systems are not rather than what they are.

questions.question: Which driving forces behind NoSQL adoption does the chapter enumerate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A need for greater scalability than relational databases can easily achieve — very large datasets or very high write throughput
A widespread preference for free and open source software over commercial database products
Specialized query operations that are not well supported by the relational model, and frustration with the restrictiveness of relational schemas
A shortage of engineers who know SQL

questions.explanation: Four forces: scalability, open source preference, specialized queries, and schema frustration.

questions.question: Define polyglot persistence and give the chapter's reasoning for it.

options.text: Relational databases will continue to be used alongside a broad variety of nonrelational datastores, because different applications have different requirements and the best technology for one use case may differ from the best for another
Every application should use exactly one database technology chosen carefully up front
All data should be migrated to a single polyglot database engine
Applications should speak multiple query languages against one store

questions.explanation: Coexistence, not replacement — the chapter's forecast for how NoSQL and SQL settle.

questions.question: Explain the electronics metaphor behind 'impedance mismatch'.

options.text: In electronics, power transfer is maximized if the impedances match; a mismatch can lead to signal reflections and other troubles — the analogue of the awkward translation layer between application objects and tables, rows and columns
Impedance is resistance, so the metaphor is about slow queries
It refers to voltage differences between components
It comes from mechanical engineering, describing friction between parts

questions.explanation: If data is stored in relational tables, an awkward translation layer is required between the objects in application code and the database model.

questions.question: Which ORM frameworks does the chapter cite, and what does it credit and deny them?

options.text: ActiveRecord and Hibernate; they reduce the amount of boilerplate code required for the translation layer, but they can't completely hide the differences between the two models
Entity Framework and SQLAlchemy; they fully eliminate the impedance mismatch
ActiveRecord and Hibernate; they make relational databases obsolete
Django ORM and Sequelize; they only help with reads

questions.explanation: Reduced boilerplate, not removed mismatch — a precise and limited claim.

questions.question: In the LinkedIn résumé example, first_name and last_name are columns on the users table, but positions, education and contact_info are not. What rule decides this?

options.text: Cardinality: first_name and last_name appear exactly once per user, so they can be columns; the others occur in varying numbers, making them one-to-many relationships
Data type: strings go in columns, everything else goes in separate tables
Query frequency: frequently-read fields become columns
Mutability: immutable fields become columns

questions.explanation: Cardinality drives the schema: exactly-once becomes a column, varying-number becomes a one-to-many relationship.

questions.question: Which three options does the chapter give for representing the résumé's one-to-many relationships in a relational schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Normalized separate tables, with a foreign key reference — the traditional approach prior to SQL:1999
Structured datatypes / XML / JSON columns, with support for querying and indexing inside those documents (Oracle, IBM DB2, MS SQL Server, PostgreSQL for XML; DB2, MySQL, PostgreSQL for JSON)
An opaque text column, letting the application interpret its structure and content
A graph edge table linking résumé sections

questions.explanation: Three escalating levels of database involvement — from fully normalized to fully opaque.

questions.question: What specifically do you lose by storing the document in a plain text column rather than a structured or JSON column?

options.text: You typically cannot use the database to query for values inside that encoded column
You lose transactional guarantees on the column
You lose the ability to replicate the column
You lose the ability to update the column

questions.explanation: The database can store it but not see into it, so all filtering and indexing on its contents must move to the application.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call a JSON representation 'quite appropriate' for a résumé, and what does it credit JSON with relative to XML?

options.text: A résumé is mostly a self-contained document; and JSON has the appeal of being much simpler than XML. Document-oriented databases named include MongoDB, RethinkDB, CouchDB and Espresso
Because JSON enforces a schema, unlike XML
Because JSON supports joins natively
Because JSON compresses better than XML

questions.explanation: Self-containedness is the structural argument; simplicity is the ergonomic one.

questions.question: Immediately after praising the JSON model, the chapter attaches two forward-pointing caveats. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: There are problems with JSON as a data encoding format, discussed in Chapter 4
The lack of a schema is often cited as an advantage, which is taken up under 'Schema flexibility in the document model'
JSON cannot represent nested structures
JSON is not supported by any relational database

questions.explanation: The chapter is careful to say only that some developers feel the JSON model reduces the impedance mismatch — it does not endorse the claim outright.

questions.question: Compare fetching a whole profile in the relational schema versus the JSON representation.

options.text: Relational requires either multiple queries (query each table by user_id) or a messy multiway join; in the JSON representation all the relevant information is in one place, so one query is sufficient — better locality
Both require exactly one query; only the result shape differs
JSON requires more queries because nested items must be resolved separately
Relational is always faster because of indexing

questions.explanation: Locality is the document model's core performance argument — and the chapter later bounds it carefully.

questions.question: Why do the one-to-many relationships in the résumé imply a tree, and what does JSON do with that fact?

options.text: Each subordinate item belongs to exactly one résumé and has no siblings pointing sideways, so the relationships form a tree — and the JSON representation makes this tree structure explicit
Because JSON only supports trees, the data must be reshaped to fit
Because foreign keys always form cycles
Because résumés are ordered documents

questions.explanation: The shape of the relationships, not the storage format, is what makes the tree.

questions.question: region_id and industry_id are IDs, not strings. Which advantages does the chapter list for standardized lists with a drop-down or autocompleter? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent style and spelling across profiles, and avoiding ambiguity where several places have the same name
Ease of updating — the name is stored in only one place, so it is easy to update across the board if it changes
Localization support — when the site is translated, standardized lists can be localized
Smaller storage footprint, which is the chapter's main stated motivation

questions.explanation: The fifth advantage on the chapter's list is better search — a search for a region can match profiles that mention a city inside it, which is not apparent from the string. Storage size is not the argument; the chapter frames the whole choice as a question about duplication, not bytes.

questions.question: The chapter reduces 'ID or text string?' to one underlying question. Which?

options.text: Duplication: with an ID, the meaningful information is stored in only one place and everything referring to it uses an ID; with text stored directly, you duplicate the human-meaningful information in every record that uses it
Performance: IDs are faster to compare
Storage: IDs consume fewer bytes
Security: IDs hide meaning from attackers

questions.explanation: The ID only has meaning within the database — that is precisely why it is stable.

questions.question: Give the chapter's argument for the stability of IDs.

options.text: Because an ID has no meaning to humans, it never needs to change — it can remain the same even if the information it identifies changes. Anything meaningful to humans may need to change, and if duplicated, all redundant copies must be updated, which incurs write overheads and risks inconsistencies
Because IDs are assigned by the database and databases never change values
Because IDs are indexed, and indexes cannot be modified
Because IDs are globally unique across all systems

questions.explanation: Meaninglessness is the source of stability — an unusually clean argument the chapter reuses later for immutable event logs.

questions.question: Define normalization as this chapter does, and state its attitude to normal forms.

options.text: Removing duplication is the key idea behind normalization; as for the various normal forms, the distinctions are of little practical interest, and a simple rule suffices — if you're duplicating values that could be stored in just one place, the schema is not normalized
Normalization means reaching at least third normal form, which the chapter treats as mandatory
Normalization means denormalizing for read performance
Normalization means enforcing a schema on write

questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly declines the normalization/denormalization debate, deferring it to Part III.

questions.question: Why does normalizing this data sit badly with the document model?

options.text: Normalizing creates many-to-one relationships, which don't fit nicely into the document model: in relational databases joins are easy, but in document databases support for joins is often weak — supported in RethinkDB, not supported in MongoDB, and only supported in predeclared views in CouchDB
Because document databases cannot store IDs
Because normalization requires a fixed schema
Because document databases have no indexes

questions.explanation: Many-to-one is the relationship shape that document models handle worst, and joins are the missing tool.

questions.question: If the database doesn't support joins, what do you do — and what does the chapter concede about this particular example?

options.text: You emulate a join in application code with multiple queries; the chapter concedes the lists of regions and industries are probably small and slow-changing enough that the application can keep them in memory — nevertheless, the work of making the join is shifted from the database to the application code
You denormalize and accept the inconsistency; the chapter says this is always fine
You switch database; the chapter says there is no workaround
You use a materialized view; the chapter says all document databases support these

questions.explanation: The concession is honest but the structural point survives it: the work moved, it did not disappear.

questions.question: What general claim does the chapter make about how application data evolves?

options.text: Data has a tendency of becoming more interconnected as features are added to applications — so a model that fits well initially may not keep fitting
Data tends to become more tree-shaped over time
Data volume grows but structure stays stable
Data becomes more normalized over time as schemas mature

questions.explanation: This is why a good initial fit is not sufficient grounds for choosing the document model.

questions.question: One user writes a recommendation for another, displayed with the recommender's name and photo. Why must the recommendation hold a reference rather than a copy?

options.text: Because if the recommender updates their photo, every recommendation they have ever written should reflect the new photo — which requires a reference to the author's profile, not a copy of the name and photo
Because copies take more disk space
Because references are faster to read
Because the document model forbids copies

questions.explanation: A copy freezes derived data that must stay live — the classic argument against denormalizing mutable, human-meaningful information.

questions.question: Which facts does the chapter state about IBM's IMS? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It was the most popular database for business data processing in the 1970s
It was originally developed for stock-keeping in the Apollo space program, and first commercially released in 1968
It is still in use and maintained today, running on OS/390 on IBM mainframes
It was the first database to implement SQL

questions.explanation: IMS used the hierarchical model, whose structure — a tree of records nested within records — is why the chapter calls it the ancestor of document databases.

questions.question: Name the network model's other name, who standardized it, and the single structural change distinguishing it from the hierarchical model.

options.text: The CODASYL model, standardized by a committee called the Conference on Data Systems Languages; it was a generalization in which a record could have multiple parents instead of exactly one
The CODASYL model, standardized by ANSI; records could have no parents
The relational model, standardized by IBM; records became unordered
The graph model, standardized by W3C; records gained labels

questions.explanation: That single relaxation is what let it model many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.

questions.question: How do CODASYL links differ from foreign keys, and what is an access path?

options.text: The links were not foreign keys but more like pointers in a programming language (while still being stored on disk); the only way of accessing a record was to follow a path from a root record along these chains of links, and that was called an access path
Links were indexed foreign keys; an access path is a query plan chosen by the optimizer
Links were symbolic names; an access path is a sorted index
Links were hashes; an access path is a partition key

questions.explanation: Pointer-chasing as the only access method is what made the model rigid.

questions.question: Describe how a CODASYL query was performed, and the admission the chapter cites.

options.text: By moving a cursor through the database, iterating over lists of records and following access paths; even CODASYL committee members admitted that this was like navigating around an n-dimensional data space
By submitting a declarative query to an optimizer, which chose the access path
By writing SQL with recursive CTEs
By issuing map and reduce functions

questions.explanation: With many-to-many relationships the application code had to keep track of all the various relationships, holding access paths in the programmer's head.

questions.question: Give the honest defence of manual access path selection, and the argument that sank it.

options.text: For: it was able to make the most efficient use of the very limited hardware capabilities of the 1970s — notably tape drives, whose seeks are extremely slow. Against: the code for querying and updating the database was complicated and inflexible, and if you had no access path to the data you wanted you had to rewrite it, making it difficult to change an application's data model
For: it was more expressive. Against: it was slower than SQL
For: it guaranteed consistency. Against: it could not scale to many machines
For: it was easier to learn. Against: it lacked tooling

questions.explanation: Under 1970s constraints, hand-tuning the path was genuinely the right call — the defence is real, and the inflexibility still killed it.

questions.question: What did the relational model do 'by contrast', and what freedoms did it grant? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It laid out all the data in the open — a relation is simply a collection of tuples, with no labyrinthine nested structures and no complicated access paths
You can read any or all of the rows in a table, selecting those that match an arbitrary condition
You can read a particular row by designating some columns as a key and matching on those, and insert a new row into any table without worrying about foreign key relationships
You can rely on the database enforcing referential integrity on every insert

questions.explanation: Foreign key constraints exist but are not required by the relational model; the query optimizer decides access at query time, and indexes are chosen at insert time.

questions.question: In what sense does a relational database still have access paths, and what is the big difference?

options.text: The query optimizer's choice of indexes and join order is effectively the access path, but it is made automatically by the query optimizer rather than by the application developer — so if you want to query your data in new ways you can just declare a new index and queries will automatically use whichever indexes are most appropriate, without changing the queries
There are no access paths in a relational database at all
Access paths are declared in the schema and fixed at table creation
Access paths are chosen by the client driver

questions.explanation: The consequence: the relational model made it much easier to add new features to applications.

questions.question: Query optimizers are complicated beasts that consumed many years of research and development effort. Reconstruct the argument that this was still the right trade.

options.text: You only need to build a query optimizer once, and then all applications that use the database can benefit from it. If you don't have one, it's easier to handcode the access paths for a particular query than to write a general-purpose optimizer — but the general-purpose solution wins in the long run
Optimizers were cheap to build compared to application code
Optimizers made hardware cheaper
Optimizers eliminated the need for indexes

questions.explanation: Build-it-once amortization — the same economic shape as the abstraction argument in Chapter 1.

questions.question: In what one aspect did document databases revert to the hierarchical model, and in what respect are they not different from relational databases?

options.text: In one aspect only: storing nested records within their parent record rather than in a separate table. For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships both are not fundamentally different — the related item is referenced by a unique identifier, called a foreign key in relational and a document reference in document databases, resolved at read time. To date, document databases have not followed the path of CODASYL
They reverted fully, including CODASYL-style access paths
They reverted in query style, becoming imperative
They reverted in ordering, making records position-dependent

questions.explanation: The precision matters: the regression is narrow, and the key mechanism for cross-references is the same in both families.

questions.question: Which differences between relational and document databases does this section explicitly set aside?

options.text: Fault-tolerance properties and handling of concurrency — the chapter concentrates only on differences in the data model
Query languages and indexing
Licensing and cost
Schema enforcement and locality

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance goes to Chapter 5 and beyond; concurrency to Chapter 7.

questions.question: Which arguments favour the document model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema flexibility
Better performance due to locality
For some applications, closeness to the data structures used by the application
Better support for joins, and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships

questions.explanation: The last one favours the relational model — those are precisely the shapes document models handle worst.

questions.question: Define shredding and state the chapter's verdict on it.

options.text: Splitting a document-like structure into multiple tables — which can lead to cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code when the data really is a tree of one-to-many relationships where typically the entire tree is loaded at once
Compressing documents before storage; the chapter recommends it
Partitioning documents across machines; the chapter calls it essential
Removing unused fields from documents; the chapter is neutral

questions.explanation: Shredding is the relational technique that the document model exists to avoid.

questions.question: State the document model's limitation on referring to nested items, and the condition under which it stops mattering.

options.text: You cannot refer directly to a nested item within a document, but instead need to say something like 'the second item in the list of positions for user 251' — much like an access path in the hierarchical model. As long as documents are not too deeply nested, that is not usually a problem
Nested items cannot be indexed at all, which is always a problem
Nested items cannot be updated, only replaced
Nested items cannot exceed three levels of depth

questions.explanation: The positional reference is the hierarchical model's access path resurfacing in miniature.

questions.question: Give the chapter's example of an application where poor join support genuinely doesn't matter.

options.text: An analytics application that uses a document database to record which events occurred at which time — many-to-many relationships may never be needed there
A social network, because friendships are symmetric
An e-commerce catalogue, because products are independent
A banking ledger, because transactions are append-only

questions.explanation: Whether weak joins matter may or may not be a problem, depending entirely on the application's relationship shapes.

questions.question: If your application does use many-to-many relationships, which two workarounds does the chapter name in a document model, and at what cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Denormalize to reduce the need for joins — but then the application code needs to do additional work to keep the denormalized data consistent
Emulate joins in application code — which moves complexity into the application and is usually slower than a join performed by specialized code inside the database
Switch to a graph query language inside the document database
Store all relationships as positional references

questions.explanation: In such cases, using a document model can lead to significantly more complex application code and worse performance.

questions.question: For highly interconnected data, how does the chapter rank the document, relational and graph models?

options.text: The document model is awkward, the relational model is acceptable, and the graph model is the most natural
The graph model is awkward, the document model is acceptable, and the relational model is most natural
All three are equally suitable
The relational model is awkward, the graph model is acceptable, the document model is most natural

questions.explanation: But it is not possible to say in general which data model leads to simpler application code — it depends on the kinds of relationships that exist between data items.

questions.question: State exactly what the chapter says about schema enforcement across document databases, JSON in relational databases, and XML in relational databases.

options.text: Document databases do not enforce any schema, and JSON support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation; XML support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation too. Arbitrary keys and values can be added, and clients have no guarantees as to what fields documents may contain
All three enforce a schema strictly
Document databases enforce schemas; relational JSON and XML support does not
None of the three offers any validation at all

questions.explanation: 'Optional' is the operative word — the capability exists, the enforcement does not by default.

questions.question: Why is 'schemaless' the wrong word, and what are the two accurate terms?

options.text: Because the code that reads the data usually assumes some kind of structure — there is an implicit schema, just not enforced by the database. The accurate terms are schema-on-read (structure is implicit and only interpreted when the data is read) and schema-on-write (the traditional relational approach, where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms to it)
Because all databases have schemas; the terms are strict-schema and loose-schema
Because schemas are always enforced at the driver level; the terms are client-schema and server-schema
Because the word is trademarked; the terms are flexible and rigid

questions.explanation: The schema does not disappear, it relocates — from the database to the reading code.

questions.question: Map schema-on-read and schema-on-write onto programming language type checking, and state the chapter's position.

options.text: Schema-on-read is analogous to dynamic (runtime) type checking; schema-on-write to static (compile-time) type checking. The chapter notes the advocates of each are passionate, it is a contentious topic, and in general there's no right or wrong answer
Schema-on-read maps to static typing; schema-on-write to dynamic typing. Static always wins
Neither maps to type checking; the analogy is with memory management
Both map to dynamic typing; the difference is only in tooling

questions.explanation: The chapter deliberately refuses to adjudicate, and instead gives the conditions under which each wins.

questions.question: You store each user's full name in one field and now want first and last name separately. What do you do in a document database?

options.text: Just start writing new documents with the new fields, and have code in the application that handles the case when old documents are read — no migration and no cutover date needed
Run a bulk migration rewriting every document
Declare a new schema version and reindex
Drop and recreate the collection

questions.explanation: The read path absorbs the heterogeneity, which is the practical meaning of schema-on-read.

questions.question: 'Schema changes have a bad reputation of being slow and requiring downtime.' How does the chapter qualify this, and what is the exception?

options.text: The reputation is not entirely deserved: most relational database systems execute ALTER TABLE in a few milliseconds. MySQL is the notable exception — it copies the entire table, which can mean minutes or even hours of downtime
The reputation is fully deserved; all databases rewrite the table
The reputation applies only to PostgreSQL
Schema changes are always instantaneous in every database

questions.explanation: Tools exist to work around the MySQL limitation, but the caveat is real.

questions.question: Between ALTER TABLE and UPDATE, which is the real performance problem, and what is the escape hatch?

options.text: UPDATE — running it on a large table is likely to be slow on any database, since every row needs to be rewritten. If that is not acceptable the application can leave the new column set to its default of NULL and fill it in at read time, like it would with a document database
ALTER TABLE — the escape hatch is to add the column in a separate table
Both are equally slow; there is no escape hatch
Neither is slow on modern hardware

questions.explanation: Note where this lands: the relational escape hatch is to behave exactly like schema-on-read.

questions.question: Which reasons does the chapter offer for data being heterogeneous enough that schema-on-read genuinely wins? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: There are many different types of objects, and it is not practical to put each type of object in its own table
The structure of the data is determined by external systems over which you have no control and which may change at any time
The dataset is too large to index
The team lacks SQL expertise

questions.explanation: The balanced conclusion: where all records are expected to have the same structure, schemas are a useful mechanism for documenting and enforcing that structure. Otherwise a schema may hurt more than it helps.

questions.question: Physically, why does a document have good locality, and what is the relational contrast?

options.text: A document is usually stored as a single continuous string, encoded as JSON, XML, or a binary variant such as MongoDB's BSON; if the application often needs the entire document there is a performance advantage to this storage locality. If data is split across multiple tables, multiple index lookups are required to retrieve it all, which may require more disk seeks
Documents are always cached in memory, unlike rows
Documents are compressed, so fewer bytes are read
Documents avoid indexes entirely

questions.explanation: Locality is a physical property of contiguous storage, not a property of the document model as such.

questions.question: Which conditions and costs bound the locality argument, and which design rules follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The advantage only applies if you need large parts of the document at the same time
The database typically needs to load the entire document even if you access only a small portion, which is wasteful on large documents

On updates the entire document usually needs to be rewritten — only modifications that don't change the encoded size can easily be performed in place. So: keep documents fairly small, and avoid writes that increase the size of a document
Locality only works on SSDs, not on spinning disks

questions.explanation: The chapter's strong verdict: these performance limitations significantly reduce the set of situations in which document databases are useful.

questions.question: Match each system to its locality mechanism: Spanner, Oracle, Bigtable.

options.text: Google's Spanner offers locality in a relational data model by letting the schema declare that a table's rows should be interleaved (nested) within a parent table; Oracle does the same with multi-table index cluster tables; the Bigtable data model (used in Cassandra and HBase) uses a column-family concept for the same purpose
All three use document nesting
Spanner uses column families; Bigtable uses interleaving; Oracle uses documents
None of them offers locality outside the document model

questions.explanation: The idea of grouping related data together for locality is not limited to the document model.

questions.question: Give the version-level facts about XML and JSON support in relational databases.

options.text: Most relational database systems other than MySQL have supported XML since the mid-2000s, including functions to make local modifications to XML documents and the ability to index and query inside them; JSON support exists in PostgreSQL since 9.3, MySQL since 5.7, and IBM DB2 since 10.5
XML since the mid-1990s in all systems; JSON only in PostgreSQL
Neither XML nor JSON is supported in relational databases
MySQL led on XML; PostgreSQL has no JSON support

questions.explanation: Given the popularity of JSON for web APIs, the chapter expects other relational databases to follow.

questions.question: What are document databases adding, and what caveat does the chapter attach?

options.text: RethinkDB supports relational-like joins in its query language, and some MongoDB drivers automatically resolve database references — but that is effectively a client-side join, likely slower than a join performed in the database since it requires additional network round-trips and is less optimized
They are adding full SQL support with no performance cost
They are adding schemas, removing the need for joins
They are adding nothing; convergence runs one way only

questions.explanation: Convergence is real but asymmetric in cost — the client-side join is not equivalent to a server-side one.

questions.question: State the chapter's verdict on convergence, and why Codd's footnote makes it a return rather than an invention.

options.text: Relational and document databases are becoming more similar over time, and that is a good thing: the data models complement each other, so applications can use whichever combination of features fits. Codd's original description of the relational model already allowed something quite similar to JSON documents within a relational schema — he called it nonsimple domains, where a value in a row need not be atomic but could be a nested relation (table). That was over 30 years before document databases arrived
The two families are diverging, and Codd predicted this
Convergence is a mistake that dilutes both models
Codd forbade nested values, making convergence a genuine invention

questions.explanation: A hybrid of the relational and document models is a good route for databases to take in the future.

questions.question: Besides a data model, what did the relational model bring, and what is the contrast with IMS and CODASYL?

options.text: A new way of querying data: SQL is declarative, whereas IMS and CODASYL both used imperative query APIs — applications typically used COBOL code to iterate over records in the database, one record at a time
Transactions; IMS and CODASYL had none
Indexes; IMS and CODASYL relied on full scans
Replication; IMS and CODASYL were single-node

questions.explanation: The declarative turn is arguably the more consequential half of the relational model's contribution.

questions.question: Define imperative and declarative query languages as the chapter does.

options.text: An imperative language tells the computer to perform certain operations in a certain order; a declarative language specifies the pattern of the data you want — what conditions the results must meet and how it should be transformed — but not how to achieve that goal, leaving the database's query optimizer to decide
Imperative languages are compiled; declarative languages are interpreted
Imperative languages use loops; declarative languages use recursion
Imperative languages are typed; declarative languages are untyped

questions.explanation: 'What, not how' is the dividing line, and the optimizer is what the gap makes room for.

questions.question: The chapter gives one obvious advantage of declarative languages, then says something else is 'more importantly' true. Which is the more important one?

options.text: That it is more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API
That it hides implementation details of the database engine, making it possible for the database system to introduce performance improvements without requiring any changes to queries
That it is easier to teach
That it can be validated statically

questions.explanation: Conciseness is the obvious win; engine evolvability without query changes is the structural one.

questions.question: The database wants to reclaim disk space by moving records around, changing the order in which animals appear. Why can it do this safely under SQL but not under imperative code?

options.text: Because SQL doesn't guarantee any particular ordering, so it doesn't mind if the order changes; with imperative code the database can never be sure whether the code is relying on the ordering or not. The fact that SQL is more limited in functionality gives the database much more room for automatic optimizations
Because SQL locks the table during compaction
Because imperative code cannot read from disk
Because SQL stores records in insertion order

questions.explanation: Less expressive power buys more freedom to optimize — the chapter's most counterintuitive line in this section.

questions.question: Which hardware trend does the chapter cite in favour of declarative languages, and what argument follows?

options.text: CPUs are getting faster by adding more cores, not by running at significantly higher clock speeds. Imperative code is very hard to parallelize because it specifies instructions that must be performed in a particular order; declarative languages specify only the pattern of the results, not the algorithm, so the database is free to use a parallel implementation
Disks are getting faster, so query plans matter less
Memory is getting cheaper, so everything fits in RAM
Networks are getting faster, favouring client-side joins

questions.explanation: The chapter cites 'The Free Lunch Is Over' for the trend.

questions.question: In CSS, the rule 'li.selected p' (p as a direct child of li.selected) declares a pattern. What does it match, and why would a p element inside a plain li not match?

options.text: It matches all p elements whose direct parent is an li element with a CSS class of selected; a p inside an li that lacks class='selected' does not match
It matches all p elements on the page regardless of parent
It matches all li elements containing any p
It matches only the first p element in the document

questions.explanation: The XSL/XPath equivalent is li[@class='selected']/p. What CSS and XSL have in common is that they are both declarative languages for specifying the styling of a document.

questions.question: The JavaScript DOM version of that styling 'is awful'. Beyond being longer, which two serious problems does the chapter identify? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It doesn't undo itself — if the selected class is removed the blue colour won't be removed even if the code is rerun, so the element stays blue until the entire page is reloaded; with CSS the browser automatically detects when the rule no longer applies

It blocks engine improvements — if you want to take advantage of a new API such as document.getElementsByClassName you have to rewrite the code, whereas browsers can improve CSS performance without breaking compatibility
It cannot select by class name at all
It only works in one browser

questions.explanation: The second problem is the database argument transplanted to the browser: declarative specifications let the engine improve underneath you.

questions.question: Is MapReduce declarative or imperative? Give the chapter's exact positioning, and the lineage of its two functions.

options.text: Neither a declarative query language nor a fully imperative query API, but somewhere in between: the logic of the query is expressed with snippets of code, which are called repeatedly by the processing framework. It is based on the map (also known as collect) and reduce (also known as fold or inject) functions from functional programming
Fully declarative, like SQL
Fully imperative, like COBOL over CODASYL
Declarative for map, imperative for reduce

questions.explanation: MapReduce is a programming model for processing large amounts of data in bulk across many machines, popularized by Google. A limited form is supported by MongoDB and CouchDB for read-only queries across many documents.

questions.question: In the MongoDB mapReduce shark query, what does the filter on shark species illustrate?

options.text: That the filter can be specified declaratively — which is a MongoDB-specific extension to MapReduce, not part of MapReduce itself
That filters must always be written inside the map function
That MapReduce cannot filter at all
That filtering happens in the reduce step

questions.explanation: The map function is then called once for every document that matches the query, with 'this' set to the document object, and emits a key and a value.

questions.question: Two observations in December 1995 have numAnimals of 3 and 4. Trace the exact calls and the result.

options.text: map is called once for each document, producing emit('1995-12', 3) and emit('1995-12', 4); then reduce('1995-12', [3, 4]) is called, returning 7
map is called once for the pair, producing emit('1995-12', 7); reduce is not called
reduce is called twice, once per document, accumulating to 7
map emits 3 and 4 as separate keys; reduce returns 3 and 4 separately

questions.explanation: Values emitted under the same key are grouped and handed to reduce once.

questions.question: What restrictions apply to map and reduce, why do they exist, and what are they still allowed to do?

options.text: They must be pure functions: they only use the data passed to them as input, cannot perform additional database queries, and must not have any side effects. These restrictions allow the database to run the functions anywhere, in any order, and rerun them on failure. They can still parse strings, call library functions and perform calculations
They must be written in JavaScript and may query the database freely
They must be idempotent but may have side effects
They must be declarative and cannot contain loops

questions.explanation: Purity is what buys relocatability, reorderability and retry — the same trade the declarative section describes.

questions.question: Why did MongoDB add the aggregation pipeline, in which version, and what is the chapter's closing judgment?

options.text: Because a usability problem with MapReduce is that you have to write two carefully coordinated JavaScript functions, often harder than writing a single query; and because a declarative query language offers more opportunities for a query optimizer to improve performance. MongoDB 2.2 added the aggregation pipeline, similar in expressiveness to a subset of SQL but with a JSON-based syntax. The moral: a NoSQL system may find itself accidentally reinventing SQL, albeit in disguise
Because MapReduce was too slow; added in MongoDB 4.0; the moral is that SQL is obsolete
Because JavaScript was deprecated; added in 3.6; the moral is to avoid pipelines
Because joins were needed; added in 2.2; the moral is that joins are unavoidable

questions.explanation: The reinvention line is the chapter's dryest verdict on the NoSQL wave.

questions.question: Using relationship shape alone, when is the document model appropriate and when does a graph become natural?

options.text: If your application has mostly one-to-many relationships (tree-structured data) or no relationships between records, the document model is appropriate. Relational databases can handle simple cases of many-to-many, but as connections within your data become more complex it becomes more natural to start modeling your data as a graph
Graphs are appropriate for tree-structured data; documents for interconnected data
The choice depends only on data volume
Graphs are always preferable once you have any many-to-many relationship

questions.explanation: A clean decision rule based purely on relationship shape, not on scale.

questions.question: Give the two kinds of objects in a graph with their synonyms.

options.text: Vertices (also known as nodes or entities) and edges (also known as relationships or arcs)
Rows (tuples) and links (pointers)
Documents (records) and references (keys)
Subjects (heads) and predicates (tails)

questions.explanation: The three canonical examples: social graphs (vertices are people, edges indicate which people know each other), the web graph (vertices are web pages, edges indicate HTML links), and road or rail networks (vertices are junctions, edges are the roads or railway lines between them). Well-known algorithms on these include shortest path and PageRank.

questions.question: The three canonical graph examples share a property. Name it, and give the chapter's 'equally powerful' alternative use.

options.text: They are homogeneous — all the vertices represent the same kind of thing. But graphs are not limited to homogeneous data: an equally powerful use is providing a consistent way of storing completely different types of objects in a single datastore, as Facebook does with one graph holding people, locations, events, checkins and comments
They are all directed, and graphs cannot be undirected
They are all acyclic, and graphs require acyclicity
They are all small enough to fit in memory

questions.explanation: Heterogeneity is where graphs beat both relational and document models on schema flexibility.

questions.question: List the two graph data models with their implementations, and the declarative query languages covered.

options.text: The property graph model (Neo4j, Titan, InfiniteGraph) and the triple-store model (Datomic, AllegroGraph and others); the declarative languages are Cypher, SPARQL and Datalog, with Gremlin as an imperative alternative and Pregel as a processing framework
The relational graph model and the document graph model; languages are SQL and Cypher only
The RDF model and the CODASYL model; the only language is SPARQL
The property graph and adjacency-list models; the only language is Gremlin

questions.explanation: The running example is Lucy from Idaho and Alain from Beaune, France — married and living in London.

questions.question: In a property graph, what does each vertex and each edge consist of?

options.text: Each vertex: a unique identifier, a set of outgoing edges, a set of incoming edges, and a collection of properties (key-value pairs). Each edge: a unique identifier, the vertex at which it starts (the tail vertex), the vertex at which it ends (the head vertex), a label describing the relationship, and a collection of properties
Each vertex: an identifier and a label. Each edge: two identifiers only
Each vertex: properties only. Each edge: a label only
Each vertex: outgoing edges only. Each edge: a weight

questions.explanation: You can think of a graph store as consisting of two relational tables, one for vertices and one for edges — with indexes on both the head and tail columns so edges can be found in both directions.

questions.question: Which are the three important aspects of the property graph model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Any vertex can have an edge connecting it with any other vertex — there is no schema that restricts which kinds of things can or cannot be associated
Given any vertex, you can efficiently find both its incoming and its outgoing edges, and thus traverse the graph both forward and backward
By using different labels for different kinds of relationships, you can store several different kinds of information in a single graph while keeping a clean data model
Edges must be traversed in the direction they were created

questions.explanation: Bidirectional traversal is exactly what CODASYL lacked, and it is what makes graph queries flexible.

questions.question: Which things does the chapter say 'would be difficult to express in a traditional relational schema' in the Figure 2-5 example? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Different kinds of regional structures in different countries — France has départements and régions, whereas the US has counties and states
Quirks of history such as a country within a country
Varying granularity of data — Lucy's current residence is specified as a city, whereas her place of birth is specified only at the level of a state
The total number of people in the graph

questions.explanation: Irregular, heterogeneous, variably-grained structure is the graph model's home territory.

questions.question: How would you extend the graph to answer 'what is safe for each person to eat', and what general property does the chapter draw from it?

options.text: Add a vertex for each allergen and an edge between a person and an allergen to indicate an allergy, then link the allergens with a set of vertices showing which foods contain which substances. Graphs are good for evolvability: as you add features, a graph can easily be extended to accommodate changes in your application's data structures
Add an allergy column to each person vertex; the property is that graphs need no schema changes
Store allergies in a separate relational table; the property is that hybrids are necessary
Encode allergies as edge properties only; the property is that edges are cheaper than vertices

questions.explanation: Evolvability by extension rather than migration.

questions.question: What is Cypher, who made it, and where does the name come from?

options.text: A declarative query language for property graphs, created for the Neo4j graph database; it is named after a character in the movie The Matrix and is not related to ciphers in cryptography
An imperative traversal API created for Titan; named after cryptographic ciphers
A triple-store query language created by the W3C
A MapReduce dialect created by Google

questions.explanation: Declarative, property-graph-oriented, and Neo4j's own.

questions.question: In Cypher, what does '(Idaho) -[:WITHIN]- (USA)' with the arrow pointing right create, precisely?

options.text: An edge labeled WITHIN, with Idaho as the tail node and USA as the head node
An edge labeled WITHIN, with USA as the tail node and Idaho as the head node
Two undirected edges between Idaho and USA
A property named WITHIN on the Idaho vertex

questions.explanation: Each vertex is given a symbolic name like USA or Idaho, and other parts of the query use those names to create edges between vertices via the arrow notation.

questions.question: A Cypher MATCH finds persons with a BORN_IN edge leading to a place connected by a chain of zero or more outgoing WITHIN edges to a Location named 'United States', and a LIVES_IN edge leading similarly to 'Europe'. What does it return?

options.text: The names of people who emigrated from the United States to Europe — both conditions must hold for the same person
The names of people born in Europe and living in the United States
All people with any BORN_IN edge
The names of all United States and Europe locations

questions.explanation: The variable-length WITHIN*0.. is what lets a birthplace at any granularity — city, state, region — roll up to the country. MATCH finds patterns in the graph, with the tail at the arrow's start and the head at its point.

questions.question: Describe the two execution strategies for that graph query, and who chooses between them.

options.text: Forward: scan all the people in the database, examine each person's birthplace and residence, and return only those meeting the criteria. Backward: start with the two Location vertices found via an index on the name property, follow all incoming WITHIN edges to find all locations inside them, and finally look for people via an incoming BORN_IN or LIVES_IN edge. As with a declarative query language, you don't need to specify such execution details — the query optimizer automatically chooses
Depth-first and breadth-first; the application chooses
Index scan and full scan; the storage engine chooses at compile time
There is only one possible strategy for graph queries

questions.explanation: Same declarative payoff as SQL: the pattern is fixed, the strategy is not.

questions.question: Can you query graph data with SQL, and what is the precise reason for the difficulty?

options.text: Yes, but with some difficulty. In a relational database you usually know in advance which joins you need; in a graph query you may need to traverse a variable number of edges before finding the vertex you're looking for, so the number of joins is not fixed in advance — a WITHIN edge may point to any kind of location: a street, a city, a district, a region, a state, and so on
No — SQL cannot express graph traversal at all
Yes, trivially — joins and traversals are equivalent
Yes, but only for undirected graphs

questions.explanation: Variable-length paths are the shape SQL handles worst, which is why recursive common table expressions exist.

questions.question: Give the form of a triple and name the parts using the chapter's example.

options.text: Three-part statements of the form (subject, predicate, object) — for example (Jim, likes, bananas), where Jim is the subject, likes is the predicate (verb), and bananas is the object
(vertex, edge, vertex) — with no predicate
(key, value, timestamp)
(table, row, column)

questions.explanation: The triple-store model is mostly equivalent to the property graph model, using different words to describe the same ideas — the chapter discusses it anyway because of the useful tools and languages built on it.

questions.question: The subject of a triple is a vertex. The object is one of two things. Which, and what does the predicate mean in each case? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A value in a primitive datatype — then the predicate and object are the key and value of a property on the subject vertex, as in (lucy, age, 33)
Another vertex in the graph — then the predicate is an edge, the subject is the tail vertex and the object is the head vertex, as in (lucy, marriedTo, alain), where marriedTo is the label of the edge
A nested triple, making the model recursive
A reference to an external RDF document

questions.explanation: The object's type is what distinguishes a property from an edge in the triple-store model.

questions.question: In Turtle notation, what does '_:someName' mean, and what does the semicolon do?

options.text: It is a local name whose meaning does not extend outside the file — used only because we otherwise have nothing to refer to the vertex by; the semicolon lets you say multiple things about the same subject. Turtle is a subset of Notation3 (N3)
It declares a globally unique URI; the semicolon ends a statement
It marks a predicate; the semicolon separates subjects
It marks a literal value; the semicolon introduces a comment

questions.explanation: Whether a predicate represents an edge or a property is determined by the object: a string literal gives a property, another vertex gives an edge.

questions.question: State the semantic web's core idea, what RDF was for, and the chapter's verdict.

options.text: The idea is simple and reasonable: websites already publish text and pictures for humans, so why not also publish machine-readable data for computers? The Resource Description Framework was intended as a consistent format for different websites to publish data in, so it could be automatically combined into a web of data. The chapter's verdict: it was overhyped in the early 2000s but not realized in practice, with a dizzying plethora of acronyms, overly complex standards proposals, and hubris — though there is also a lot of good work that came out of it
The idea was to replace HTML with XML; RDF was a styling language; the chapter calls it a success
The idea was to build a global graph database; RDF was a storage engine; the chapter calls it premature
The idea was to standardize SQL across the web; RDF was a protocol; the chapter is neutral

questions.explanation: Crucially, the triple-store data model is completely independent of the semantic web: Datomic is a triple-store making no such claim (it technically uses 5-tuples, the two extra fields being metadata for versioning). Triples can be a good internal data model even if you have no interest in publishing RDF.

questions.question: Why are RDF subjects, predicates and objects often URIs, and must they resolve?

options.text: Because RDF is designed for internet-wide data exchange: using a URI as a predicate means that if you combine your data with someone else's and they used the same word with a different meaning, you won't get a conflict, since their predicate is really a different URI. The URI doesn't necessarily need to resolve to anything — it is simply a namespace, and you can specify the prefix once at the top of the file
Because RDF requires every identifier to be fetchable over HTTP
Because URIs compress better than strings
Because URIs are required by SPARQL's grammar

questions.explanation: RDF also has an XML form (RDF/XML), but Turtle/N3 is preferable as it is much easier on the eyes, and tools like Apache Jena can convert between formats.

questions.question: Expand SPARQL, give its pronunciation, and state its historical relationship to Cypher.

options.text: SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language, pronounced 'sparkle'; a query language for triple-stores using the RDF data model. It predates Cypher, and since Cypher's pattern matching is borrowed from SPARQL, they look quite similar
StructuredParallel Query Language, pronounced 'spar-cue-el'; it postdates Cypher
Semantic Property And Relationship Query Language; unrelated to Cypher
SPARQL Pattern And RDF Query Layer; Cypher predates it

questions.explanation: The borrowing runs from SPARQL to Cypher, not the other way round.

questions.question: Comparing the emigration query in SPARQL and Cypher, which equivalences does the chapter draw? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The same query is even more concise in SPARQL than in Cypher; variables start with a question mark in SPARQL
Because RDF doesn't distinguish between properties and edges but just uses predicates for both, you can use the same syntax for matching properties as for edges
SPARQL cannot express variable-length paths
SPARQL requires an explicit join clause

questions.explanation: The chapter's closing judgment: even if the semantic web never happens, SPARQL can be a powerful tool for applications to use internally.

questions.question: 'Are graph databases the second coming of CODASYL in disguise?' Which differences does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Schema — CODASYL had a schema specifying which record type could be nested within which other record type; a graph has no such restriction, and any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex

Reaching a record — in CODASYL the only way was to traverse one of the access paths; in a graph you can refer directly to any vertex by its unique ID, or use an index to find vertices with a particular value

Ordering — CODASYL children were an ordered set, so the database had to maintain that ordering and applications had to worry about positions; in a graph, vertices and edges are not ordered, so you only sort results when making a query
Storage — CODASYL stored links on disk whereas graph databases keep the entire graph in memory

questions.explanation: The answer to the question is No. The fourth genuine difference is query style: in CODASYL all queries were imperative, whereas graph databases can be imperative but also support high-level, declarative query languages. In-memory storage is not one of the differences — CODASYL links were pointer-like but still stored on disk, and graph databases store on disk too.

questions.question: When was Datalog studied, why does the chapter include it, and where is it actually used?

options.text: It is a much older language than SPARQL or Cypher, studied extensively by academics in the 1980s and less well known among software engineers; the chapter includes it because it provides the foundation that later query languages build upon. In practice it is used in Datomic, and Cascalog is a Datalog implementation for querying large datasets in Hadoop
It was invented in the 2000s as an RDF language and is used only in academic prototypes
It dates from the 1970s and is used inside PostgreSQL's optimizer
It was created for Neo4j and predates Cypher by two years

questions.explanation: Datomic uses a Clojure S-expression syntax while the chapter's examples use Prolog syntax; there is no functional difference. Datalog is a subset of Prolog.

questions.question: How does Datalog's notation relate to the triple-store model?

options.text: It is similar to the triple-store model, generalized a bit: instead of writing a triple as (subject, predicate, object) it is written as predicate(subject, object)
It writes triples as subject(predicate, object)
It uses a completely unrelated relational notation
It uses object(subject, predicate)

questions.explanation: A small notational move that makes rules composable.

questions.question: Cypher and SPARQL jump in right away with SELECT. What does Datalog do instead, and what is the payoff?

options.text: Datalog takes a small step at a time: we define rules that tell the database about new predicates, which aren't triples stored in the database but are derived from data or from other rules. Rules can refer to other rules, just as functions can call other functions or recursively call themselves, so complex queries can be built up a small piece at a time
Datalog compiles to SQL, so the payoff is portability
Datalog runs imperatively, so the payoff is control
Datalog defines schemas first, so the payoff is validation

questions.explanation: Composition and reuse, at the cost of a less direct route to a simple answer.

questions.question: State the convention for Datalog variables and the condition under which a rule applies.

options.text: Words that start with an uppercase letter are variables; a rule applies if the system can find a match for all predicates on the righthand side of the :- operator, and then it's as though the lefthand side of the :- was added to the database, with variables replaced by the values they matched
Variables start with a question mark; a rule applies when any predicate on the right matches
Variables start with an underscore; rules apply unconditionally
Variables are quoted strings; rules apply only to stored triples

questions.explanation: Matching all right-hand predicates is what makes rule application a conjunction, enabling the step-by-step build-up.

questions.question: State the honest cost and benefit of the Datalog approach.

options.text: It requires a different kind of thinking than other query languages, and is less convenient for simple one-off queries; but it is a very powerful approach because rules can be combined and reused across different queries, and it can cope better if your data is complex
It is always more convenient and never harder to think in
It is faster but less expressive than SQL
It is only suitable for one-off queries

questions.explanation: Reuse pays off as query complexity grows, not on the first simple query.

questions.question: Reconstruct the historical arc the summary gives.

options.text: Data started out being represented as one big tree (the hierarchical model), but that wasn't good for representing many-to-many relationships, so the relational model was invented to solve that problem. More recently, developers found that some applications don't fit well in the relational model either, and NoSQL went in two main directions
Data started relational, moved to hierarchical for performance, then to graphs
Data started as graphs, was flattened to trees, then normalized into tables
Data started as documents, then trees, then tables

questions.explanation: Each transition is driven by a relationship shape the previous model handled badly.

questions.question: State the two NoSQL directions and the use case each targets, in the summary's own terms.

options.text: Document databases target use cases where data comes in self-contained documents and relationships between one document and another are rare; graph databases go in the opposite direction, targeting use cases where anything is potentially related to everything
Key-value stores target scale; column stores target analytics
Document databases target interconnected data; graph databases target self-contained data
Both target the same use case with different syntax

questions.explanation: The two poles of relationship density.

questions.question: The summary concedes that one model can be emulated in terms of another. Why doesn't that collapse the three models into one?

options.text: Because emulation proves expressive equivalence, not fitness: graph data can be represented in a relational database, but the result is often awkward. That's why we have different systems for different purposes, not a single one-size-fits-all solution — all three models are widely used today, and each is good in its respective domain
Because emulation is impossible for graphs
Because relational databases cannot store nested data
Because the models have different consistency guarantees

questions.explanation: The concrete measurement of awkwardness is the chapter's 4-lines-of-Cypher versus 29-lines-of-SQL comparison.

questions.question: Name the property document and graph databases have in common, its benefit, and the qualification the summary attaches.

options.text: They typically don't enforce a schema, which can make it easier to adapt applications to changing requirements. However, your application most likely still assumes that data has a certain structure; it's just a question of whether the schema is explicit (enforced on write) or implicit (handled on read)
They both support joins natively, which improves locality
They both guarantee strong consistency, which simplifies application code
They both store data as trees, which improves cache behaviour

questions.explanation: The qualification is the chapter's whole point about 'schemaless': the assumption never goes away, only its enforcement point moves.

questions.question: Which of the following did the chapter discuss that are NOT database query languages? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: CSS
XSL/XPath
Cypher
Datalog

questions.explanation: The chapter covered SQL, MapReduce, MongoDB's aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL and Datalog as database query languages, and drew interesting parallels with CSS and XSL as declarative document-styling languages.

questions.question: Match each specialized domain the summary mentions to its requirement and named system.

options.text: Genome data needs sequence-similarity searches — matching one very long string against a large database of similar but not identical strings, which none of the databases described here can handle, hence specialized software like GenBank
Genome data needs full-text search, handled by GenBank
Particle physics needs sequence-similarity search, handled by the LHC
Full-text search needs custom hardware, handled by information retrieval systems

questions.explanation: Also mentioned: particle physics, where the Large Hadron Collider's hundreds of petabytes have driven decades of custom solutions to stop hardware cost spiralling out of control; and full-text search, a kind of data model used alongside databases, with information retrieval touched on in Chapter 3 and Part III.

questions.question: What does the chapter say the next chapter will discuss?

options.text: Some of the trade-offs that come into play when implementing the data models described in this chapter
Replication and partitioning of distributed data
Encoding formats and schema evolution
Transactions and isolation levels

questions.explanation: Chapter 3 moves one layer down: from the model to storage and retrieval.
